name: Habits
summary: What helps you check off what you have done, come back after a miss, and use a tracker at your own pace.
lead:
In the morning a person is trying to leave on time; in the evening they are trying to remember what they managed to do; a week later they look at an empty square and decide whether to carry on at all. At each of those stages the tracker has to help in a different way. A prompt leads to the action, a check-in records the fact, the history helps make sense of the previous days.

The weak spot appears when keeping track means taking on another habit — long spells of filling in the app and correcting its calendar. The important question for this category: does the tracker help a person carry on with ordinary life after a distraction, a miss or a change of schedule?

cover.alt: A woman lays the next stone in a path beside a flowering plant.

audiencesArt.alt: Seen from above: three people reading, stretching and watering a plant.

audiences.title: Getting ready and taking the next step
audiences.body: Some people find it hard to start getting ready in the morning; others find it hard not to get distracted between actions. What helps here is a clear order, a visible next step and the chance to carry on from where you stopped. The level of detail in a schedule is worth matching to the particular person: the same sequence of pictures can be useful to a child and to an adult alike.

audiences.title: Watching yourself over the long run
audiences.body: Some people want to check off walks or reading every day. Others are better served by remembering the date of the last clean-up, seeing rest among their workouts, or allowing for a shift schedule. History starts to help when its records match the way the person actually lives, and when changes to goals don’t rewrite the past.

audiences.title: Agreeing with another person
audiences.body: A couple can choose a shared habit, a parent can prepare a schedule, a professional can go over a client’s records before a meeting. These relationships have different boundaries. Who draws up the plan, who carries it out and who can see the detail is better settled before anyone is invited into a shared tracker.

sections.title: First, make the action manageable
sections.intro: A tracker steps into a day that already exists, with work, commuting and distractions in it. The first question is at which moment it will be of use. After an action is done, what is needed is a fast check-in; while getting ready, what may be needed is a prompt about what to do next.

observations.title: Start with one real action
passages: Instead of the habit, you can quietly start servicing the tracker: choosing the styling, filling in settings, moving plans around. One review author explicitly describes filling it in as another task there is not enough attention for. The more often that path has to be repeated, the more every extra field counts.

One positive review values an app that isn’t trying to be a thousand things at once. The first encounter can be built around a single action of the person’s own, showing what tomorrow’s entry will look like. Advanced capabilities can be offered once it is clear what they are missing.

The record itself comes in different kinds. A checkmark answers the question “was it done”, while a photo and a note help recall the circumstances. These are different jobs: adding a detailed diary to a simple counter makes sense only when the person really does go back to that information.

quotes.text: I've tried a lot of habit trackers, but there is almost always TOO much to fill in that it made me not want to use them. The process of filling everything in felt like it needed to be a habit in itself. My ADHD brain gets too distracted.
I just downloaded this app, and love it so far! I enjoy the simplicity of it and that it's not trying to be 1000 things at once. The UI is intuitive and pleasant to look at.

placements.title: Choose a different format for the record
placements.body: A photo food diary is a neighboring scenario, not a required feature of a tracker. It makes sense when a person needs to recall the circumstances rather than count completed actions.

observations.title: Check it off before it slips your mind
passages: A widget or a watch is useful at one particular moment: the action is already done, opening the phone is awkward, and an entry put off can get lost among other things. In one positive review the path is described as literally a few taps.

A reminder solves the neighboring job — it brings attention back to what hasn’t been done yet. One author values several alerts for a habit, because he tends to put the first one off. It helps here to tie the alert to a clear choice: do it now, move it, or record the result. The frequency is for the person to match to their own day.

After the check-in, the feedback still has to be checked. An author who uses the watch complains specifically about a bar that looks like progress but doesn’t reflect it. Fast entry loses its point if it isn’t clear whether the result was saved. A person should see the saved check-in immediately and be able to undo a mistaken tap.

quotes.text: A lot of thought went into this app and it shows. So easy to use and a pleasant experience to mark goals complete. Tap the widget, tap the goal, and done. Or use Siri Shortcuts. This is perfect.

So intuitive, and easy to get ramped right away! I love how you can add multiple reminders for the same habit. Especially handy for people like me that have a tendency to hit the snooze button and actually this app feels like a to-do list and a habit tracker combined.

I like that I can complete habits from my watch. I won't stick to it otherwise. But the watch interface could be better. The little widget bar that looks like it should show progress doesn't. It always looks like 2/3 of my habits are done.

art.alt: A woman with a bag at an open door holds out her wrist with a watch on it.

placements.title: Finish the entry on whichever device suits
placements.body: An entry like that is worth trying against the place where the action happens: a walk, a workout, or getting ready in the evening. Speed matters more than the number of input methods.

observations.title: Give the check-in a pleasant ending
passages: The daily gesture can be enjoyable in itself: hold the button down, feel the response, see what you have done. In a review of a simple tracker, the sound and the vibration are mentioned together with the short action. The expressiveness here is built into the use rather than requiring a separate set of rules to work out.

Another author describes a small sense of pride after each check-in. That experience is no basis for judging the usefulness of animation in general. A pleasant first experience can change when the same gesture is repeated every day.

A person can choose an expressive response or a quiet confirmation. That shows which option stays comfortable in everyday use. A separate game system is worth adding once its role in a particular practice is clear.

quotes.text: For the most part, I really like this app. There's no ads and the developers don't collect your data. The app is habit tracking in its simplest form. You just open the app and hold the button, no fluff. The sounds and haptics are great.

Life changing! I originally downloaded this app to build habits. Checking each habit I've completed feels so satisfying. It's that small sense of pride that keeps you going. No matter how small that change seems, when you incorporate into your life, it matters.

observations.title: Prompt what to do right now
passages: While getting ready, a task list answers only part of the questions. You still have to work out which action comes next and how much time is left before you leave. One review particularly values the prompts that keep updating when the next step starts and when the whole sequence ends.

Order matters even when several tasks are set for the same time. One author asks to be able to sort them within that shared slot. For a product this is a reason to test a small real scenario: what happens if the first step drags on, if one item is already done, or if the person gets distracted halfway through?

The form of the prompt is a choice too. One adult user tells how a visual schedule designed for children suited him. So it is more useful to check whether a person recognizes the action from the picture and understands the transition than to decide the whole interface by age. For family use there is one more job — getting the prepared schedule onto the device where it will be used.

quotes.text: This is one of the best apps i've ever used. I've tried so many routine apps, timers, but this one has been the most helpful so far. the constantly updating reminders of when the next task will start and when it will all end are IMMENSELY helpful.

This app is a gem and I really like it worth every penny. I have three small suggestions that I would LOVE to be implemented. Make it so that tasks that are due at the same time or in the same time frame be able to be sorted in a specific order.

I am an adult with inattentive ADHD and DID. I've used many scheduling and to-do list apps for adults that were very functional but didn't work for me. Then I looked to see if there were apps for ADHD and there were, but lucky me! I found this one meant for children that works perfectly for my brain.

art.alt: Morning actions line up as a path that leads out of the house.

placements.title: Get the schedule to where it is carried out
placements.body: In a family the person who draws up the schedule and the person who uses it can be different people. Delivering the current sequence matters more than one shared calendar for everyone.

sections.title: Then, learn to carry on
sections.intro: A few neatly filled-in days still don’t show whether the tool suits you for the long haul. The real test begins with a forgotten entry, a changed schedule or a break. What matters is how those show up in the history and what a person sees on coming back.

observations.title: Choose what exactly to count
passages: Not every repeating task needs to be tied to a daily square. For household upkeep it can be enough to know how long it has been since the last time. One author uses the counter precisely for periodic cleaning and other household chores, even though the app was designed for a different job.

In another situation the same number helps a person see the time since they started quitting a habit. One author specifically values having it on the widget. The mechanic looks the same, but the meaning of a new event differs: for cleaning it simply starts the next interval, while in a personal history it can be felt far more sharply.

One of the reviews links the reset to shame. That is a reason to design the recording of a new event carefully: keep the previous periods, allow the date to be corrected, and let an explanation be added. The counter shows part of the experience, but it doesn’t explain the reason for the break.

quotes.text: As someone with ADHD, I find this app to be a game changer to keep up with life admin, cleaning, and anything that happens on a periodic schedule. While it was designed to help quit habits like smoking, I find it to be incredibly useful for tracking anything periodic.

I've used a couple of these apps on the few times I've tried to quit drinking and this one is reaaalllly helping me honestly. I love the layout and customization options. It looks really nice and the widget that shows me how many days I've been sober is so helpful.

the basic idea of counting the days is extremely helpful. when you relapse it almost feels guilty to reset the counter, especially when you've gone far along. once you get in the habit of using this, the guilt really turns something on in your brain.

placements.title: Keep the periods after a new event
placements.body: A new count should not erase the previous periods. The history helps tell one more event apart from the loss of the whole journey so far.

observations.title: Tell rest, a miss and a forgotten entry apart
passages: An empty square can mean different things: the action didn’t happen, the person took a pause, or they simply didn’t enter the result. One author asks for the streak to be kept during illness and a vacation. This is a question about the rules of the history, and it is worth settling before the first break.

A forgotten entry calls for something else. In one review a person wants to enter three tasks completed yesterday, and that takes fifteen taps. The work is already done; now it is awkward entry that stops it being recorded. Being able to open the day you need and fix several check-ins keeps the diary meaningful.

There is also a request for an explicit “not done”: the morning is over, and the morning action is no longer going to happen. That is how a closed day can be told apart from an unfilled one. These states are there so people can read their own history honestly, not to punish them for an empty square.

With shift work, the day boundary is added on top: calendar midnight can fall in the middle of the working day. That is a separate schedule setting. It doesn’t replace a pause or a late check-in; it determines which day an action belongs to.

quotes.text: This app is generally really good and it's helped me a lot since getting it. But there's one pretty significant feature missing, and it's an option to pause habits and not lose your streak. For example if you become sick or go on a vacation.

Really like this app, but it desperately needs an easier way to edit habits for past dates. Presently, if I want to add 3 tasks I completed yesterday, that requires 15 taps! WAY too cumbersome. The best option would be to simply allow users to edit any day directly.

I like this app but there is one problem. I would like it to be possible to mark habits as not completed. For example, if I have a morning routine and I haven't done some habit, and the morning has already passed, then it's clear that I can't complete it now.

art.alt: A person rests among the days already saved: a break does not wipe out the path behind them.

placements.title: Come back without recreating the habit
placements.body: Coming back after a miss is a part of using a tracker in its own right. It has to keep the earlier records meaningful.

placements.title: Tie the day to the person’s schedule
placements.body: For a night shift, defining the start of the day correctly is more useful than adding one more alert at an awkward time.

placements.title: Show the program’s rules in advance
placements.body: A program with a fixed term needs rules that are clear in advance for how a day ends and how a new attempt begins.

observations.title: Keep a history worth coming back to
passages: A month overview helps show what gets lost in today’s list: where actions repeated, where the gaps were, what changed over time. A visual form can make that easier to read. One author says specifically that thinking in pictures and using a simple, visual tracker suits him.

Another user has been coming back to the app for many years and values a quick way to record behavior. Here the entry and the overview work together: the history exists because it can be kept up. It is worth testing not only the attractive chart but the step from it to a particular day.

Over the years the habits themselves change. One author says he periodically reviews his list and wants to use it on different devices. So a change of goal is better stored along with its date: the old check-ins have to stay legible. Export and history transfer are worth testing on accumulated records: do the dates, the explanations and the previous goals survive?

quotes.text: i'm a sucker for pretty apps and that's what this is. im a very visual thinker and i love using everyday for habit tracking. its so simple and intuitive to use and i got lost in reading all the research articles and videos etc. that were provided.

I've been using this app on and off for years now but have been using it very consistently for a couple years straight now and it has had a tremendous positive impact on my life. Having a really quick and easy way to log my patterns and behaviors is incredible.

I have used this app for years. I don't even know how many. I feel like at least 10 years. Every so often I reevaluate my listed habits — update etc. That is when I think it would be awesome to have it on my phone and iPad.

placements.title: Check that what has accumulated is safe
placements.body: The accumulated history becomes a value in its own right. It is worth keeping along with the dates when goals changed, so that past check-ins stay legible.

sections.title: And choose the support that fits
sections.intro: A personal history can become the basis for a conversation with someone close or with a professional. But access to the check-ins changes the relationship with the tracker. So shared use is worth building around a specific agreement: why the records are being looked at, and how to respond to them.

observations.title: Agree on what exactly you are doing together
passages: A shared tracker can start with an ordinary conversation: a couple choose the habits they want to work on. The shared record then continues an agreement that already exists. It is worth establishing what the participants need to see in each other and what kind of response they count as support.

For friends a game can serve the same purpose. In one review the participants know they could cheat the system but don’t want to: they are interested in carrying on together. That detail helps separate mutual involvement from outside control. The mere visibility of check-ins doesn’t yet explain what holds a particular group together.

There is another side: one person describes how other people’s results make you justify your own workout. That example from a sports app is useful as a warning about comparison. It doesn’t prove that every shared mechanic is harmful, but it shows why the visibility of all results must not be made mandatory.

Working with a coach is different from swapping check-ins with friends. Here the records help prepare for a particular meeting, and access is worth limiting to the actions that were agreed. What has to be checked is what changed in the conversation, not how many reminders the client received.

quotes.text: I'm not one to review apps but this one has made me so excited to use, I had to write a review to express how much I recommend it. After discussing with my boyfriend some of the habits we both want to develop and work on, we were looking for something we could both use and track together.

My friends and I use this to stay motivated and keep each other accountable. I know it's just an RPG that can easily be cheated, but somehow we don't want to cheat and the game keeps us engaged. Just bought an annual subscription which I rarely do.

As a long-time endurance athlete, it's easy to get sucked into comparison. My friend did this, I'm falling behind. Oh, my run today was really slow, I need to make an excuse in my Strava workout description so people have context and don't think I'm slow.

art.alt: Two friends pass a watering can between them, each tending their own bed.

placements.title: Start from what the couple agreed
placements.body: A shared habit starts from an agreement about support. Full visibility of someone else’s diary isn’t required for that.

placements.title: Prepare for the conversation with a professional
placements.body: For a meeting with a professional, selected records and explanations for the period can be enough, without access to the whole personal diary.

conclusion.title: The main test is the day after a miss
conclusion.body:
For an existing tracker the most concrete improvement is to make coming back easier. Open a past day, fix a few check-ins, tell a pause apart from a missed action, and move on to the next action. This is not a promise to build a habit: the app is only removing an obstacle that its own rules created.

For a new product it is worth picking one rhythm of life: shift work, a family getting ready in the morning, or quick personal check-ins. They make different demands of the schedule and of other people’s involvement. Show a person their own history with a break in it and watch whether they can carry it on without an explanation. If they first have to work through streaks, penalties and settings, the new mechanic has become a separate job again.
